title: Grafana on AWS -- Amazon Managed Grafana vs self-hosted
exp: Before building a single dashboard, you need to choose how Grafana itself runs on AWS. This decision affects IAM design, cost, and how much operational burden you take on.
pts: Amazon Managed Grafana (AMG): a fully managed workspace -- AWS and Grafana Labs jointly operate the Grafana server, patching, and scaling. You never SSH into anything.

AMG authentication: integrates with IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) or SAML, so your existing corporate identity provider controls who can log in -- no separate Grafana user database to manage.
AMG pricing is per active user per month (editor vs viewer tiers), billed through AWS Marketplace -- predictable but can add up for large viewer populations.

Self-hosted alternative: run Grafana OSS on EC2, ECS/Fargate, or via Docker. Full control over plugins (some community plugins aren't available in AMG) and no per-user licensing cost, at the price of patching and uptime being your responsibility.

Critical IAM detail: the Grafana WORKSPACE itself needs an IAM role to query CloudWatch -- this is separate from the IAM Identity Center login that controls who can access Grafana. Without this service role attached, every CloudWatch panel fails with an authorization error.
AMG workspace creation specifies which data source types it's allowed to connect to (CLOUDWATCH, PROMETHEUS, XRAY, etc.) -- this is a workspace-level allowlist, not just a per-data-source setting.

VPC connectivity: if a data source lives inside a private VPC (a self-hosted Prometheus, an RDS-backed metrics store), AMG needs VPC configuration (subnets, security groups) to reach it -- public CloudWatch and X-Ray don't need this.

r: Grafana's own user DB (or your own SSO setup)
Teams needing specific plugins or zero licensing cost

qa.q: What is the key IAM detail people miss when setting up Amazon Managed Grafana?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** The Grafana WORKSPACE needs its own IAM role with CloudWatch read permissions -- this is separate from IAM Identity Center, which only controls who can log into Grafana. People often set up SSO correctly, log in successfully, then hit 'access denied' on every CloudWatch panel because they forgot to attach a service role (like CloudWatchReadOnlyAccess) to the workspace itself.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Cloud infrastructure APIs use declarative control planes. Terraform tracks infrastructure in a state DAG, resolving dependency ordering before making cloud provider REST API calls. IAM policies evaluate explicit DENYs before ALLOWs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Hardcoding credentials or missing remote state locks (S3 + DynamoDB) in team pipelines can lead to state corruption and credential leaks in source code.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Infrastructure-as-Code enforces repeatable, audited infrastructure deployments, but requires strict state lock management and PR plan validation to prevent accidental resource deletion.

qa.q: When would you choose self-hosted Grafana over Amazon Managed Grafana?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Self-hosted when: you need a community plugin not supported in AMG, you want zero per-user licensing cost and are willing to own patching, or you need Grafana inside a fully air-gapped/on-prem environment. AMG when: you want zero operational burden, you already use IAM Identity Center for SSO, and predictable per-user billing is acceptable. For most teams building on AWS, AMG's reduced operational burden outweighs the licensing cost.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: What does the data_sources allowlist on an AMG workspace control?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It's a workspace-level setting listing which data source TYPES the workspace is permitted to connect to (CLOUDWATCH, PROMETHEUS, XRAY, ATHENA, etc.) -- not a per-instance configuration. You must include a type in this list before you can add an individual data source of that type inside the Grafana UI. It's a coarse-grained guardrail set at provisioning time, separate from the fine-grained IAM permissions on the workspace role.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Functional guards (CanActivateFn) execute in the router's dependency injection context using inject(). They evaluate sequentially before component instantiation. Returning UrlTree cancels the current navigation and triggers a redirect in a single router atomic tick.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Guards that make un-cached HTTP calls to auth endpoints block every single sub-route navigation. Fix: cache auth state in a Signal or BehaviorSubject service so guards check in-memory state synchronously.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Functional guards eliminate class boilerplate and are tree-shakeable, but require careful usage of inject() strictly inside synchronous execution contexts.

qa.q: Why would a self-hosted Grafana instance need VPC configuration but a CloudWatch-only AMG workspace might not?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** CloudWatch and X-Ray are public AWS service APIs reachable over the internet (or a VPC endpoint) -- AMG can query them without any special networking. But if your data source is a Prometheus server or an RDS instance running inside a private VPC with no public endpoint, Grafana needs network connectivity into that VPC -- via VPC configuration (subnet IDs, security group) on the AMG workspace, or simply by running self-hosted Grafana on an EC2 instance already inside that VPC.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.
